A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CARES and retain matching methods, experiments, and results. All 12 pages of v2 and 14 pages of v3, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, selector ablations, latency measurements, and predicted-resolution distributions.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds teacher-agreement measurements, proxy-feature comparisons, token statistics, and additional autoregressive-selector results.

M1.justification: The truncated SmolVLM classifier, Granite-Docling LoRA alternative, sufficiency-labeling rule, training objectives, and probability-weighted continuous resolution selection are unchanged. The additional teacher and feature comparisons do not establish a revision to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same four-source training set and report nine evaluation benchmarks in Table 2. MMMU, RealWorldQA, InfoVQA, and MathVista are newly named in v3's evaluation prose but already have results in v2. The additional analyses vary models and procedures within retained task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds CARES-AR to the GPT-4o comparison; v2 evaluated this variant with Granite-Vision and InternVL3 only. Appendix A.5 also compares Qwen-family and SmolVLM features through downstream performance, extending beyond their existing selector-classification comparison in Table 3.

E3.justification: New analyses specify a shared 1,000-example teacher comparison, a Qwen2.5-VL-3B downstream feature comparison, and token-composition calculations assuming 100 text tokens. Existing training settings remain unchanged. Table 5's accompanying prose changes averaging from five to nine benchmarks, but its caption still says five and its values are unchanged; the effective aggregation is unresolved.

E4.justification: v3 substantially extends the supplementary analyses by testing agreement between Granite-Vision-2B and Qwen3-VL-235B resolution labels, testing downstream sensitivity to proxy–target feature mismatch, and analyzing prompt lengths and architecture-dependent visual-token composition. The earlier ablations, latency analysis, and resolution distributions are retained. Fixed-resolution controls already appeared in v2 Figure 2.

E5.justification: Table 11 introduces ± quantities for downstream scores, whereas v2 reports point estimates. Their statistical meaning, run counts, and seeds are unspecified, so this establishes additional uncertainty reporting without establishing repeated runs or a particular estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Matched values in Tables 2–6 and the appendix latency table are retained. Substantial additions include teacher-agreement results, token statistics, and four-task proxy-feature results. The new GPT-4o + CARES-AR row reports average score 0.66 and 78% API-cost reduction, versus 0.69 for native GPT-4o and 0.68 with 55% reduction for CARES. Figure 5 shows 943/1,000 agreements, contradicting the new prose claim of more than 95%.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds analytical token-count functions and explicit patch, merging, and capped-tiling assumptions for Qwen2.5-VL, AnyRes, and InternVL3, explaining their different scaling regimes. The core sufficiency definitions and continuous-selection mathematics are unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The main preprocessing and model-agnostic contributions remain unchanged. The abstract and contributions now claim up to 78% savings averaged across nine benchmarks, replacing the earlier 80%/85% headline figures, and qualify token dominance as concerning prefill. However, Table 2's 78% entry represents GPT-4o CARES-AR API-cost savings with lower accuracy, limiting support for presenting it as accuracy-preserving compute reduction.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations that sufficient-resolution judgments are shared across teachers and that transferable coarse visual–textual cues explain tolerance to proxy-feature mismatch. Appendix A.1 explains architecture-dependent token dominance. Limitations newly identify untested model perturbations and annotation noise; the earlier fine-detail and single-image, single-turn boundaries remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly documents the Qwen2.5-VL tokenizer, inclusion of answer choices and instruction suffixes in prompt counts, and architecture-specific constants used for visual-token estimates. Main training hyperparameters, autoregressive implementation details, existing H100 latency settings, and project-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for four already evaluated benchmarks, Granite 4.0 Vision, model perturbations, and annotation noise. Section 2 and the positioning of CARES as complementary preprocessing before token compression remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most retained prose is unchanged apart from local wording, benchmark-count, and caption edits. v3 inserts analysis subsections, fixes appendix numbering and stray text, and removes the separate Future Directions list. These are bounded structural edits rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the displays with a first-page token-composition plot, a teacher-confusion heatmap, and four appendix tables. Table 9 tabulates the fixed-resolution score pattern already plotted in v2 Figure 2. Existing diagrams, latency tables, and histograms are retained and repositioned; Table 2 gains a row and expanded caption, and the latency plot receives annotation and bubble-size adjustments.

improvement.justification: The teacher-agreement and proxy-feature analyses provide useful evidence for previously untested aspects of CARES's model-agnostic premise, while token statistics make its efficiency motivation more assessable. These are limited gains: the agreement claim conflicts with Figure 5, the 78% headline obscures an API-cost/accuracy tradeoff, Table 5 has inconsistent averaging descriptions, and Appendix A.3 leaves its setting as a placeholder. The additions improve support without resolving these reporting weaknesses.
